newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean president's son questioned in loan scandal.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean president's son questioned in loan scandal.

text.p: South Korean state prosecutors on Friday questioned a son of President Kim Young-sam in connection with a loan scandal that has badly damaged the government's credibility.

A prosecution official said Kim Hyun-chul was questioned over a libel complaint he filed on Tuesday against six opposition politicians who accused him of peddling influence in giving loans to the failed Hanbo Steel Co.
Among the six from the main opposition National Congress for New Politics are party spokesman Chung Dong-young, his deputy Sul Hoon and three other members of parliament.
"The prosecutors will also look into various suspicions raised about Mr Kim Hyun-chul," a prosecution official told Reuters.
Kim Hyun-chul, the president's second son, has said he had nothing to do with five trillion won ($5.8 billion) of loans that Hanbo Steel racked up before being declared insolvent on January 23.
The Hanbo scandal has eaten into the political credibility of President Kim who has sought to project an image as an anti-graft crusader since tooking office in 1993.
On Wednesday, prosecutors indicted 10 people, including Hanbo Group founder Chung Tae-soo and three close aides to the president, on bribery and embezzlement charges in the scandal.
Hanbo Steel is the flagship of the Hanbo Group, South Korea's 14th-biggest conglomerate.

Those in President Kim's inner circle who were indicted included former home affairs minister, Kim Woo-suk, who resigned last week shortly before being arrested for bribery. He was the third cabinet minister to resign under a cloud of corruption.
The other two were lawmakers Hong In-gil and Hwang Byung-tai, who were key members of a faction in the ruling New Korea Party that backed Kim's rise to power.

Prosecutors said they might also question six opposition politicians who Hyun-chul said defamed him. But apart from them, the prosecution had no plan to summon more political figures in connection with the scandal.
Kwon Roh-kap, a top aide to opposition leader Kim Dae-jung, has also been charged with accepting bribes from the Hanbo founder.
Opposition parties have demanded a new probe, saying prosecutors had only revealed "a few feathers and not the body" of the case.
Kim Jong-pil, president of the United Liberal Democratic Party, repeated an opposition call for special legislation to allow independent prosecutors to restart the probe.
"The president must realise that uncovering the full truth about Hanbo is the only way to resolve the current problems," he told parliament.

The National Congress's vice president Shin Nak-yun said on Thursday, her party would seek a televised hearing during a separate parliamentary probe, for which a special committee had already been formed in the National Assembly.

Senior prosecutor Choi Byung-koog said the prosecution had run into problems because key evidence had been destroyed, including Hanbo's account books before 1993. Cash bribes were extremely difficult to track down, he added.
The prosecution is relying heavily on testimony by Hanbo Group founder Chung Tae-soo, one of those indicted along with former company treasurer Kim Jong-kook.
